New Perspectives on the Unimodality of Domination Polynomials

Mohamed Omar Address: Department of Mathematics & Statistics. York University. 4700 Keele St. Toronto, Canada. M3J 1P3 Email address: omarmo@yorku.ca
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

The domination polynomial of a graph GG is given by D⁡(G,x)=∑k=0ndk​(G)​xkD(G,x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}d_{k}(G)x^{k} where dk​(G)d_{k}(G) records the number of kk-element dominating sets in GG. A conjecture of Alikhani and Peng asserts that these polynomials have unimodal coefficient sequences. We develop three complementary perspectives that strengthen existing tools for resolving the conjecture. First, we view dominating sets as transversals of the closed neighborhood hypergraph. Motivated by the relationship between the unimodality of a polynomial and its roots, we use this perspective to expand on known root phenomena for domination polynomials. In particular, we obtain a bound on the modulus of domination roots that is linear in the maximum degree of a graph, improving related exponential bounds of Bencs, Csikvári and Regts. The hypergraph viewpoint also yields explicit combinatorial formulas for top coefficients of D⁡(G,x)D(G,x), extending formulas in the literature and offering fruitful ground for combinatorial approaches to the unimodality conjecture. Second, we strengthen the coefficient-ratio method of Beaton and Brown. This includes tightening their inequalities, and combining a union bound for non-dominating kk-element sets with an overlap correction based on spanning trees. This produces a new parameter τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) measuring maximal pairwise neighborhood overlap and yields an overlap-corrected sufficient criterion for unimodality. Third, we prove that the domination polynomial of threshold graphs are log-concave, and hence unimodal, by a planar network argument from total positivity. This offers a new tactic for resolving the unimodality of hereditary graph classes.

Key words and phrases: 
dominating sets, domination polynomial, domination roots, unimodality, hypergraph independence polynomial, threshold graphs, total positivity

05C31, 05C69

1. Introduction

Let GG be a finite simple undirected graph with vertex set V⁡(G)V(G), and n=|V⁡(G)|n=|V(G)|. A set S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is dominating if every vertex is either in SS or adjacent to a vertex of SS. Let dk​(G)d_{k}(G) denote the number of dominating sets of size kk. Alikhani and Peng [1] introduced the domination polynomial given by

(1.1) D⁡(G,x)=∑k=0ndk​(G)​xk,D(G,x)=\sum_{k=0}^{n}d_{k}(G)x^{k},

which records dominating sets of varying sizes in its coefficients. Domination polynomials have since been studied from several points of view, including recurrence relations and splitting formulas [13], domination equivalence and reconstruction questions [4], and the distribution of roots [2, 3, 6].

The domination polynomial packages dominating set information in a way that parallels several other graph polynomials. The independence polynomial counts independent sets by size, while the domination polynomial counts hitting sets for closed neighborhoods. Matching polynomials and independence polynomials often exhibit strong analytic phenomena (real-rootedness, log-concavity, sharp zero-free regions) that can be leveraged for coefficient questions. Domination polynomials are less rigid, but their coefficient sequences still appear to have robust shape. One reason is that dominating sets form a large and highly correlated family: in most graphs, once a set is moderately large, it is likely to dominate many vertices simultaneously. The normalized coefficients rk​(G)r_{k}(G) from (1.2) make this probabilistic intuition precise.

Another source of structure comes from graph operations. For disjoint unions one has D⁡(G1∪G2,x)=D⁡(G1,x)​D​(G2,x)D(G_{1}\cup G_{2},x)=D(G_{1},x)\,D(G_{2},x), and for joins there are similar explicit formulas, see [13]. Such identities allow one to build large families of graphs with controllable domination polynomials from smaller pieces. However, unimodality is not automatically preserved under all natural operations, and controlling the interaction between pieces remains delicate. This is one reason it is helpful to have several complementary approaches to the unimodality conjecture of Alikhani and Peng [1], which is one of the long standing conjectures on these polynomials.

Conjecture 1 ([1]).

For every finite graph GG, the domination sequence (dk​(G))k=0n(d_{k}(G))_{k=0}^{n} is unimodal.

In many settings unimodality is a shadow of a stronger property such as log-concavity or real-rootedness, but domination polynomials do not generally enjoy either: even when GG is a tree, domination polynomials can have nonreal roots and need not be log-concave [2]. Existing proofs of unimodality therefore tend to rely on more delicate combinatorial or probabilistic structure, and even basic families such as trees remain challenging.

The current evidence for Conjecture 1 comes from several directions. First, the conjecture holds for a number of dense families where domination is “easy” in the sense that a random set of size about n/2n/2 almost surely dominates. This includes graphs of sufficiently large minimum degree [2]. Second, the conjecture has been verified for certain highly structured graph classes, including complete multipartite graphs [2] and other families with explicit domination recurrences. It has also been verified for many special families of trees, graphs with maximum degree at most 400400, and persists on other highly specialized families (see [8]). On the other hand, sparse graphs are genuinely subtle. For example, for trees the domination number can be linear in nn, and the family of dominating sets reflects fine local structure (leaves, supports, and branching). From this point of view, Conjecture 1 for trees is reminiscent of the long-standing conjecture that the independence polynomial of a tree is unimodal. In both cases, the central coefficients are governed by many competing local configurations.

It is therefore natural to look for methods that are sensitive to local neighborhood structure but still yield global control. The three perspectives developed here aim to do exactly that: Perspective 1 translates domination into a hypergraph independence problem and imports global analytic information. Perspective 2 measures the failure of domination by local avoidance events but corrects for their overlaps. Perspective 3 imports theory from total positivity to establish log-concavity and hence unimodality. Before detailing the results from each perspective, we detail pertinent relevant results in the literature.

One of the most general results to date is due to Beaton and Brown [2]. They introduced the normalized coefficients

(1.2) rk​(G):=dk​(G)(nk),r_{k}(G):=\frac{d_{k}(G)}{\binom{n}{k}},

interpretable as the probability that a uniformly random kk-element subset of V⁡(G)V(G) is dominating. They proved that rk​(G)r_{k}(G) is nondecreasing in kk. Since (nk)\binom{n}{k} is increasing for k≤⌊n/2⌋k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor, this implies that dk​(G)d_{k}(G) is increasing for k≤⌊n/2⌋k\leq\lfloor n/2\rfloor.

The same paper provides a criterion that forces the tail of the domination sequence to be nonincreasing. In one convenient form, if k≥n/2k\geq n/2 and rk​(G)≥n−kk+1r_{k}(G)\ \geq\frac{n-k}{k+1}, then dk​(G)≥dk+1​(G)≥⋯≥dn​(G)d_{k}(G)\geq d_{k+1}(G)\geq\cdots\geq d_{n}(G). Together with the monotonicity of rk​(G)r_{k}(G), it follows that verifying this inequality at k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil implies unimodality with mode ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil.

A different but closely related line of work concerns the roots of domination polynomials. Since D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) has nonnegative coefficients it has no positive real roots, but it can have complex roots with positive real part and with arguments close to 00. On the real axis, the picture is now essentially complete: Beaton and Brown proved that the closure of the set of real domination roots is (−∞,0](-\infty,0] [3]. For complex roots, Bencs, Csikvári, and Regts used Wagner’s weighted subgraph counting polynomial to obtain a uniform disk containing all roots when the maximum degree is bounded, and they related domination roots to roots of edge cover polynomials [6]. These questions are important due to the relationship between log-concavity, unimodality, and roots of a polynomial.

The purpose of this paper is to develop three complementary perspectives that interact naturally with these themes. The first perspective is that dominating sets can be interpreted in terms of independent sets in an associated hypergraph. For a graph GG, consider the hypergraph ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} whose hyperedges are the closed neighborhoods N⁡[v]N[v] for v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). Dominating sets then are precisely complements of hypergraph independent sets in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}. This gives the identity D⁡(G,x)=xn​I​(ℋG,1/x),D(G,x)=x^{n}I(\mathcal{H}_{G},1/x), where I⁡(ℋG,x)I(\mathcal{H}_{G},x) is the hypergraph independence polynomial. While the identity is elementary, it is powerful because it allows us to transport recent sharp zero-free results for bounded degree hypergraph independence polynomials to domination polynomials. We use this to obtain a bound on domination roots that is linear in the maximum degree of GG, and to prove the existence of a uniform root-free neighborhood of a positive ray for all graphs with bounded maximum degree. On the coefficient side, the identity shows that dn−k​(G)d_{n-k}(G) counts kk-element independent sets in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}, and for small kk this yields explicit formulas in terms of local low degree configurations. As a representative result we give a full expression for dn−3​(G)d_{n-3}(G) valid for all graphs, keeping track of isolated vertices and small components.

The second perspective is an extension of the Beaton-Brown ratio method. Since rk​(G)r_{k}(G) is the probability that a random kk-element set is dominating, one wants to bound the probability of failure. A basic union bound produces a quantity σk​(G)\sigma_{k}(G) such that rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G). We use this to strengthen and generalize the degree lower bound condition of Beaton and Brown that guarantees unimodality. We then observe that this bound ignores overlaps among the events that avoid specific neighborhoods; in graphs with repeated neighborhoods those overlaps are substantial. To mitigate for this, we introduce an overlap correction based on spanning trees, encoded in a new term τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G), yielding rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)+τk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G)+\tau_{k}(G). This leads to a new sufficient criterion for unimodality at k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil.

The third perspective shows how unimodality can be inherited from existing theory in enumerative combinatorics. We show that polynomials that are sums of shifted binomials whose exponents follow a prescribed “staircase” structure are log-concave and hence unimodal. This is established by using a planar network argument from total positivity, exploiting classic Lindström-Gessel-Viennot theory. We use this in turn to prove that a ubiquitous and well-studied class of graphs, threshold graphs, have unimodal domination polynomials.

The paper is organized into three main sections corresponding to these perspectives, preceded by a brief preliminaries section and followed by a conclusion emphasizing open directions for extending these methods.

2. Preliminaries

We introduce preliminaries that will be used throughout. For v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), denote by N⁡[v]N[v] the closed neighborhood of vv, which consists of vv and all vertices adjacent to vv. The minimum and maximum degrees of a graph GG are δ⁡(G)\delta(G) and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G), respectively. We write i⁡(G)i(G) for the number of isolated vertices and ℓ⁡(G)\ell(G) for the number of leaves.

Throughout our work, we use two results from [2] as black boxes. These statements will be used repeatedly; we refer to (ii) as the Beaton-Brown tail criterion.

Proposition 2.

[2] Let GG be a graph on nn vertices and define rk​(G)r_{k}(G) as in (1.2).

(i) The sequence r0​(G),r1​(G),…,rn​(G)r_{0}(G),r_{1}(G),\dots,r_{n}(G) is nondecreasing.

(ii) If k≥n/2k\geq n/2 and rk​(G)≥(n−k)/(k+1)r_{k}(G)\geq(n-k)/(k+1) then dk​(G)≥dk+1​(G)≥⋯≥dn​(G)d_{k}(G)\geq d_{k+1}(G)\geq\cdots\geq d_{n}(G). In particular, if the inequality holds at k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil, then D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) is unimodal with mode ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil.

We also recall basic hypergraph terminology. A hypergraph ℋ\mathcal{H} consists of a finite vertex set V⁡(ℋ)V(\mathcal{H}) and a collection of hyperedges E⁡(ℋ)⊆2V⁡(ℋ)E(\mathcal{H})\subseteq 2^{V(\mathcal{H})}. An independent set in ℋ\mathcal{H} is a set U⊆V⁡(ℋ)U\subseteq V(\mathcal{H}) that contains no hyperedge as a subset. The independence polynomial is

I⁡(ℋ,x)=∑U⊆V⁡(ℋ)U​independentx|U|.I(\mathcal{H},x)=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}U\subseteq V(\mathcal{H})\\ U\ \text{independent}\end{subarray}}x^{|U|}.

The maximum degree Δ⁡(ℋ)\Delta(\mathcal{H}) is the maximum number of hyperedges containing a single vertex. For a graph GG, a corresponding hypergraph of relevance in this article is the closed neighborhood hypergraph ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}. This hypergraph has vertex set and edge set given by

V⁡(ℋG)=V⁡(G),E⁡(ℋG)={N⁡[v]:v∈V⁡(G)}.V(\mathcal{H}_{G})=V(G),\qquad E(\mathcal{H}_{G})=\{N[v]:v\in V(G)\}.

Dominating sets in GG are exactly the transversals of ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}, and this reduction is standard in domination-set enumeration [12]. More explicitly we see that taking complements, S⊆V⁡(G)S\subseteq V(G) is dominating if and only if U=V⁡(G)∖SU=V(G)\setminus S is independent in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} because a dominating set SS must intersect N⁡[v]N[v] nontrivially for every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G). Summing over all such UU gives

(2.1) D⁡(G,x)=∑S​ dominating in ​Gx|S|=∑U​ independent in ​ℋGxn−|U|=xn​I​(ℋG,1/x).D(G,x)=\sum_{S\text{ dominating in }G}x^{|S|}=\sum_{U\text{ independent in }\mathcal{H}_{G}}x^{n-|U|}=x^{n}I(\mathcal{H}_{G},1/x).
Example 3.

Let GG be the path graph on vertex set V⁡(G)={1,2,3,4}V(G)=\{1,2,3,4\} with edge set E⁡(G)={12,23,34}E(G)=\{12,23,34\}. The closed neighborhoods of GG give rise to the closed neighborhood hypergraph ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} with vertex set V⁡(ℋG)=V⁡(G)V(\mathcal{H}_{G})=V(G) and hyperedge set E⁡(ℋG)={12,34,123,234}E(\mathcal{H}_{G})=\{12,34,123,234\}. The dominating sets in GG are

{1,3},{1,4},{2,3},{2,4},{1,2,3},{1,2,4},{1,3,4},{2,3,4},{1,2,3,4}\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\},\{1,2,3\},\{1,2,4\},\{1,3,4\},\{2,3,4\},\{1,2,3,4\}

so D⁡(G,x)=x4+4​x3+4​x2D(G,x)=x^{4}+4x^{3}+4x^{2}. The independent sets in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} are

∅,{1},{2},{3},{4},{1,3},{1,4},{2,3},{2,4}\emptyset,\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{4\},\{1,3\},\{1,4\},\{2,3\},\{2,4\}

so I⁡(ℋG)=4​x2+4​x+1I(\mathcal{H}_{G})=4x^{2}+4x+1. We see that x4​I​(ℋG,1/x)=x4⋅(4x2+4x+1)=D⁡(G,x)x^{4}I(\mathcal{H}_{G},1/x)=x^{4}\cdot\left(\frac{4}{x^{2}}+\frac{4}{x}+1\right)=D(G,x).

The reciprocity identity (2.1) governs our findings in Perspective 1. We make an important note that will be useful throughout: a vertex u∈V⁡(G)=V⁡(ℋG)u\in V(G)=V(\mathcal{H}_{G}) lies in a hyperedge N⁡[v]N[v] if and only if v∈N⁡[u]v\in N[u], so uu belongs to exactly degG⁡(u)+1\deg_{G}(u)+1 hyperedges. Consequently

(2.2) Δ⁡(ℋG)=Δ⁡(G)+1.\Delta(\mathcal{H}_{G})=\Delta(G)+1.

3. Perspective 1: the closed neighborhood hypergraph

3.1. Top coefficients from low degree structure.

The identity (2.1) implies that dn−k​(G)d_{n-k}(G) counts the kk-element independent sets of ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}, equivalently the complements of (n−k)(n-k)-element dominating sets. For small kk, independence in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} is governed by small hyperedges, hence by low degree vertices in GG. It is this that allows us to access top coefficients of D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) readily.

Two immediate consequences are worth recording. If 0≤k≤δ⁡(G)0\leq k\leq\delta(G) then every kk-element subset U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G) is independent in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}, because every hyperedge has size at least δ⁡(G)+1\delta(G)+1. Therefore

(3.1) dn−k​(G)=(nk)(0≤k≤δ⁡(G)).d_{n-k}(G)=\binom{n}{k}\qquad(0\leq k\leq\delta(G)).

Similarly, for k=δ⁡(G)+1k=\delta(G)+1 a (δ⁡(G)+1)(\delta(G)+1)-element subset fails to be independent if and only if it is exactly a hyperedge N⁡[v]N[v] with deg⁡(v)=δ⁡(G)\deg(v)=\delta(G). Thus

(3.2) dn−δ⁡(G)−1​(G)=(nδ⁡(G)+1)−|{N⁡[v]:deg⁡(v)=δ⁡(G)}|.d_{n-\delta(G)-1}(G)=\binom{n}{\delta(G)+1}-\bigl|\{N[v]:\deg(v)=\delta(G)\}\bigr|.

These identities are straightforward consequences of (2.1).

More generally, for a fixed integer kk, the coefficient dn−k​(G)d_{n-k}(G) can be computed by inclusion-exclusion over those vertices vv with |N⁡[v]|≤k|N[v]|\leq k, since only those hyperedges can be contained in a kk-element subset of V⁡(G)V(G). In graph language this means that dn−k​(G)d_{n-k}(G) is determined entirely by the local structure around vertices of degree at most k−1k-1, together with the way their closed neighborhoods overlap. Theorem 4 is the first nontrivial instance of this principle. One conceptual advantage of phrasing the computation in ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} is that the relevant configurations are naturally organized by the sizes of the hyperedges rather than by ad hoc graph cases.

For k=1k=1 and k=2k=2 one can easily recover the familiar formulas

(3.3) dn−1​(G)=n−i⁡(G),d_{n-1}(G)=n-i(G),

and

(3.4) dn−2​(G)=(n2)−(i⁡(G)​(n−1)−(i⁡(G)2)−e1​(G)),d_{n-2}(G)=\binom{n}{2}-\Bigl(i(G)(n-1)-\binom{i(G)}{2}-e_{1}(G)\Bigr),

where e1​(G)e_{1}(G) denotes the number of edges incident to a leaf. These appear, for example, in [4] (see also the survey discussion there for additional sources).

We now give an explicit expression for dn−3​(G)d_{n-3}(G) in terms of configurations of degree at most 22, valid for all graphs. Earlier formulas typically assumed the graph has no isolated vertices and no K2K_{2} components; see [4].

Theorem 4.

Let GG be a graph on nn vertices. Then

dn−3​(G)\displaystyle d_{n-3}(G) =(n3)−(i⁡(G)​(n−12)+ℓ⁡(G)​(n−2)+n2​(G))\displaystyle=\binom{n}{3}-\Bigl(i(G)\binom{n-1}{2}+\ell(G)(n-2)+n_{2}(G)\Bigr)
+((i⁡(G)2)⁡(n−2)+i⁡(G)​ℓ​(G)+e2​(G)​(n−2)+s⁡(G)+m⁡(G)+t22​(G))\displaystyle\quad+\Bigl(\binom{i(G)}{2}(n-2)+i(G)\ell(G)+e_{2}(G)(n-2)+s(G)+m(G)+t_{22}(G)\Bigr)
(3.5) −((i⁡(G)3)+i⁡(G)​e2​(G)+p3​(G)+c3​(G)),\displaystyle\quad-\Bigl(\binom{i(G)}{3}+i(G)e_{2}(G)+p_{3}(G)+c_{3}(G)\Bigr),

where: n2​(G)n_{2}(G) is the number of vertices of degree 22, e2​(G)e_{2}(G) is the number of connected components isomorphic to K2K_{2}, s⁡(G)s(G) is the number of unordered pairs of leaves with a common neighbor, m⁡(G)m(G) is the number of edges joining a leaf to a degree 22 vertex, t22​(G)t_{22}(G) is the number of unordered pairs of degree 22 vertices with equal closed neighborhood, p3​(G)p_{3}(G) is the number of connected components isomorphic to the path P3P_{3}, and c3​(G)c_{3}(G) is the number of connected components isomorphic to K3K_{3}.

Proof.

By (2.1), dn−3​(G)d_{n-3}(G) is the number of 33-element independent subsets in the hypergraph ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G}. Equivalently, if U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G) with |U|=3|U|=3 and UU is called bad when it contains a hyperedge N⁡[v]N[v] as a subset, then

dn−3​(G)=(n3)−|{U⊆V⁡(G):U​ is bad }|.d_{n-3}(G)=\binom{n}{3}-|\{U\subseteq V(G):U\text{ is bad }\}|.

A hyperedge N⁡[v]N[v] has size deg⁡(v)+1\deg(v)+1, so N⁡[v]⊆UN[v]\subseteq U with |U|=3|U|=3 forces deg⁡(v)≤2\deg(v)\leq 2. For each vertex vv with deg⁡(v)≤2\deg(v)\leq 2, let AvA_{v} denote the event that N⁡[v]⊆UN[v]\subseteq U. Then UU is bad if and only if at least one event AvA_{v} occurs. We compute the number of bad UU by inclusion-exclusion over the events AvA_{v}.

If vv is isolated, then N⁡[v]={v}N[v]=\{v\} and AvA_{v} occurs precisely when v∈Uv\in U. For each isolated vv there are (n−12)\binom{n-1}{2} choices for UU, hence isolated vertices contribute i⁡(G)​(n−12)i(G)\binom{n-1}{2} to the count of bad sets. If vv is a leaf, with unique neighbor ww, then N⁡[v]={v,w}N[v]=\{v,w\} and AvA_{v} occurs precisely when {v,w}⊆U\{v,w\}\subseteq U, leaving n−2n-2 choices for the third element. Summing over all leaves contributes ℓ​(G)​(n−2)\ell(G)(n-2). If vv has degree 22 with neighbors uu and ww, then N⁡[v]={u,v,w}N[v]=\{u,v,w\} and there is exactly one 33-element set containing it, so each vertex of degree 22 contributes 11, giving n2​(G)n_{2}(G). The total single event contribution is therefore

i⁡(G)​(n−12)+ℓ⁡(G)​(n−2)+n2​(G).i(G)\binom{n-1}{2}+\ell(G)(n-2)+n_{2}(G).

Next we adjust this count by considering Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} for distinct vertices uu and vv of degree at most 22. Because |U|=3|U|=3, this intersection can occur only when |N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|≤3|N[u]\cup N[v]|\leq 3, and in each admissible case the resulting UU is forced or nearly forced. If uu and vv are distinct isolated vertices, then N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]={u,v}N[u]\cup N[v]=\{u,v\} and Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} occurs precisely when {u,v}⊆U\{u,v\}\subseteq U. There are n−2n-2 choices for the third vertex, contributing (i⁡(G)2)⁡(n−2)\binom{i(G)}{2}(n-2) over all such pairs. If uu is isolated and vv is a leaf, then Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} forces UU to contain uu and the edge N⁡[v]N[v], hence UU is uniquely determined. The number of choices is i⁡(G)​ℓ​(G)i(G)\ell(G). If uu and vv are leaves, then |N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|≤3|N[u]\cup N[v]|\leq 3 forces either that they are adjacent (forming a K2K_{2} component) or that they share a common neighbor. If they are adjacent then N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]={u,v}N[u]\cup N[v]=\{u,v\} and Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} occurs when UU contains uu and vv; the third element is arbitrary among the remaining n−2n-2 vertices. Summing over K2K_{2} components contributes e2​(G)​(n−2)e_{2}(G)(n-2). If they are not adjacent but share a common neighbor ww, then N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]={u,v,w}N[u]\cup N[v]=\{u,v,w\} and Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} forces U={u,v,w}U=\{u,v,w\} uniquely. The number of such unordered pairs of leaves is s⁡(G)s(G). If one vertex is a leaf and the other has degree 22, then for |N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|≤3|N[u]\cup N[v]|\leq 3 to hold the leaf must be adjacent to the vertex of degree 22. In this case the union of neighborhoods equals the closed neighborhood of the vertex of degree 22 and again forces UU uniquely. Each edge joining a leaf to a vertex of degree 22 yields one such intersection, contributing m⁡(G)m(G). Finally, if uu and vv are both vertices with degree 22, then Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v} can occur only if N⁡[u]=N⁡[v]N[u]=N[v], in which case UU is forced to equal this common neighborhood. No other pair of vertices can yield Au∩AvA_{u}\cap A_{v}, because any other combination forces |N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|≥4|N[u]\cup N[v]|\geq 4. (i⁡(G)2)⁡(n−2)+i⁡(G)​ℓ​(G)+e2​(G)​(n−2)+s⁡(G)+m⁡(G)+t22​(G).\binom{i(G)}{2}(n-2)+i(G)\ell(G)+e_{2}(G)(n-2)+s(G)+m(G)+t_{22}(G).

Finally we adjust for triple intersections Au∩Av∩AwA_{u}\cap A_{v}\cap A_{w}. This can occur only when U=N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]∪N⁡[w]U=N[u]\cup N[v]\cup N[w] has size at most 33, and therefore when the three vertices form a union of connected components in GG whose closed neighborhoods stay within the triple. There are exactly four possibilities. If u,v,wu,v,w are all isolated, then the intersection holds for the unique set U={u,v,w}U=\{u,v,w\}, contributing (i⁡(G)3)\binom{i(G)}{3} to the count. If two of the vertices form a K2K_{2} component and the third is isolated, then the intersection corresponds to choosing a K2K_{2} component and an isolated vertex, contributing i⁡(G)​e2​(G)i(G)e_{2}(G). If {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} forms a P3P_{3} component, then all three closed neighborhoods are contained in {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} and the intersection contributes p3​(G)p_{3}(G). If {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\} forms a K3K_{3} component, the same holds and contributes c3​(G)c_{3}(G). No other triple intersections occur, because any other configuration forces at least one closed neighborhood to contain a vertex outside {u,v,w}\{u,v,w\}.

Applying inclusion–exclusion yields (3.5). ∎

The same method extends in principle to dn−4​(G)d_{n-4}(G) and beyond, but the number of admissible local configurations grows quickly. For dn−4d_{n-4} one already encounters interactions among degree 33 neighborhoods, and a tractable closed formula typically requires structural restrictions (such as excluding isolated vertices and K2K_{2} components); see [4] for a detailed discussion of such formulas and their use in domination equivalence.

3.2. Roots via zero-free regions for I⁡(ℋ,x)I(\mathcal{H},x).

We now turn to roots. The identity (2.1) reduces domination roots to zeros of a hypergraph independence polynomial. Recent work gives sharp, uniform zero-free regions for I⁡(ℋ,x)I(\mathcal{H},x) in terms of the hypergraph maximum degree [5]. Using (2.2), these results transfer to bounds on roots of domination polynomials in terms of Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G).

Our first result gives a modulus bound that is linear in Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) for domination roots. For comparison, Bencs, Csikvári, and Regts proved that if GG has no isolated vertices and Δ⁡(G)≤Δ\Delta(G)\leq\Delta, then all roots of D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) lie in the disk |z|≤2Δ+1|z|\leq 2^{\Delta+1} with radius bounded by an exponential in Δ\Delta [6].

Theorem 5.

Let GG be a graph with maximum degree Δ=Δ⁡(G)≥1\Delta=\Delta(G)\geq 1. If zz is a complex root of D⁡(G,x)D(G,x), then |z|<e⁡(Δ+1).|z|<e(\Delta+1).

Proof.

Let z≠0z\neq 0 satisfy D⁡(G,z)=0D(G,z)=0. Bencs and Buys proved that if ℋ\mathcal{H} is a hypergraph with maximum degree at most MM, then I⁡(ℋ,λ)≠0I(\mathcal{H},\lambda)\neq 0 whenever

(3.6) |λ|<λs​(M):=(M−1)M−1MM,|\lambda|<\lambda_{s}(M):=\frac{(M-1)^{M-1}}{M^{M}},

and that this radius is optimal [5]. By (2.2), the hypergraph ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} has maximum degree Δ⁡(ℋG)=Δ+1\Delta(\mathcal{H}_{G})=\Delta+1, so applying the Bencs and Buys result with M=Δ+1M=\Delta+1 gives that I⁡(ℋG,λ)≠0I(\mathcal{H}_{G},\lambda)\neq 0 for all |λ|<λs​(Δ+1)=ΔΔ/(Δ+1)Δ+1|\lambda|<\lambda_{s}(\Delta+1)=\Delta^{\Delta}/(\Delta+1)^{\Delta+1}. By (2.1), since zz is a root of D⁡(G,z)=0D(G,z)=0, 1/z1/z is a root of I⁡(ℋG,x)=0I(\mathcal{H}_{G},x)=0, so (3.6) implies |1z|≥ΔΔ(Δ+1)Δ+1,\left|\frac{1}{z}\right|\geq\frac{\Delta^{\Delta}}{(\Delta+1)^{\Delta+1}}, and therefore |z|≤(1+1Δ)Δ⋅(1+Δ)|z|\leq\left(1+\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{\Delta}\cdot(1+\Delta). It is classical that (1+1Δ)Δ<e\left(1+\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{\Delta}<e for Δ≥1\Delta\geq 1, and the result follows. ∎

We next prove that for bounded degree graphs, domination roots avoid a uniform neighborhood of a positive ray beyond an explicit threshold. This is a complex analytic strengthening of the trivial observation that there are no positive real roots: it rules out roots approaching the positive real axis with modulus bounded away from zero, uniformly over all graphs of bounded maximum degree.

Theorem 6.

Fix an integer Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2 and define TΔ=(Δ−1)Δ+1ΔΔ.T_{\Delta}=\frac{(\Delta-1)^{\Delta+1}}{\Delta^{\Delta}}. There exists an open set ΩΔ⊆ℂ\Omega_{\Delta}\subseteq\mathbb{C} containing the ray (TΔ,∞)(T_{\Delta},\infty) such that for every graph GG with Δ⁡(G)≤Δ\Delta(G)\leq\Delta one has D⁡(G,z)≠0D(G,z)\neq 0 for all z∈ΩΔz\in\Omega_{\Delta}.

Proof.

Let M=Δ+1M=\Delta+1. Bencs and Buys proved that for every integer M≥3M\geq 3 there exists an open neighborhood UMU_{M} of the interval (0,λc​(M))(0,\lambda_{c}(M)), where λc​(M)=(M−1)M−1(M−2)M,\lambda_{c}(M)=\frac{(M-1)^{M-1}}{(M-2)^{M}}, such that I⁡(ℋ,λ)≠0I(\mathcal{H},\lambda)\neq 0 for all λ∈UM\lambda\in U_{M} and all hypergraphs ℋ\mathcal{H} with Δ⁡(ℋ)≤M\Delta(\mathcal{H})\leq M [5]. Since Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2 implies M=Δ+1≥3M=\Delta+1\geq 3, we may apply this with M=Δ+1M=\Delta+1. Writing LΔ:=λc​(Δ+1)=ΔΔ/(Δ−1)Δ+1L_{\Delta}:=\lambda_{c}(\Delta+1)=\Delta^{\Delta}/(\Delta-1)^{\Delta+1}, we have LΔ=1/TΔL_{\Delta}=1/T_{\Delta}. Define

ΩΔ:={z∈ℂ∖{0}:1/z∈UM}.\Omega_{\Delta}:=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}:1/z\in U_{M}\}.

Since inversion is continuous on ℂ∖{0}\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}, the set ΩΔ\Omega_{\Delta} is open. Because UMU_{M} contains (0,LΔ)(0,L_{\Delta}), the set ΩΔ\Omega_{\Delta} contains (TΔ,∞)(T_{\Delta},\infty). Now let GG satisfy Δ⁡(G)≤Δ\Delta(G)\leq\Delta. Then Δ⁡(ℋG)≤Δ+1\Delta(\mathcal{H}_{G})\leq\Delta+1 by (2.2). If z∈ΩΔz\in\Omega_{\Delta} then 1/z∈UM1/z\in U_{M}, hence I⁡(ℋG,1/z)≠0I(\mathcal{H}_{G},1/z)\neq 0. By (2.1), D⁡(G,z)=zn​I​(ℋG,1/z)≠0D(G,z)=z^{n}I(\mathcal{H}_{G},1/z)\neq 0. ∎

The next theorem extracts a uniform angular separation around the positive real axis beyond any fixed radius r>TΔr>T_{\Delta}. It is a compactness argument made quantitative via the stability of inversion near the positive real axis.

Theorem 7.

Fix Δ≥2\Delta\geq 2 and r>TΔr>T_{\Delta}. There exists θ=θ⁡(Δ,r)>0\theta=\theta(\Delta,r)>0 such that for every graph GG with Δ⁡(G)≤Δ\Delta(G)\leq\Delta the domination polynomial D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) has no root zz satisfying |z|≥r|z|\geq r and |arg⁡(z)|<θ|\argu(z)|<\theta.

Proof.

Let M=Δ+1M=\Delta+1 and UMU_{M} be the open set from the proof of Theorem 6. Since r>TΔr>T_{\Delta}, we have 1/r<LΔ1/r<L_{\Delta}, where LΔ=1/TΔL_{\Delta}=1/T_{\Delta}. Consider the compact interval

K:=[0,1r]⊆ℝ.K:=\left[0,\frac{1}{r}\right]\subseteq\mathbb{R}.

Because UMU_{M} is open and contains KK, there exists ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that the open ε\varepsilon-neighborhood of KK is contained in UMU_{M}. In other words, if λ∈ℂ\lambda\in\mathbb{C} satisfies dist⁡(λ,K)<ε\dist(\lambda,K)<\varepsilon, then λ∈UM\lambda\in U_{M}. Now choose θ>0\theta>0 such that

(3.7) 2r​sin⁡(θ/2)<ε.\frac{2}{r}\sin(\theta/2)<\varepsilon.

We show that for any z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} satisfying |z|≥r|z|\geq r and |arg⁡(z)|<θ|\argu(z)|<\theta, D⁡(G,z)≠0D(G,z)\neq 0. Write z=|z|​ei​ϕz=|z|e^{i\phi} with |ϕ|<θ|\phi|<\theta. Then 1z=1|z|​e−i​ϕ.\frac{1}{z}=\frac{1}{|z|}e^{-i\phi}. Let t:=1/|z|t:=1/|z|, so 0<t≤1/r0<t\leq 1/r and hence t∈Kt\in K. We estimate

|1z−t|=t​|e−i​ϕ−1|=t⋅2​sin⁡(|ϕ|/2)≤2|z|​sin⁡(θ/2)≤2r​sin⁡(θ/2)<ε\left|\frac{1}{z}-t\right|=t\left|e^{-i\phi}-1\right|=t\cdot 2\sin(|\phi|/2)\leq\frac{2}{|z|}\sin(\theta/2)\leq\frac{2}{r}\sin(\theta/2)<\varepsilon

by (3.7). Thus dist⁡(1/z,K)<ε\dist(1/z,K)<\varepsilon, so 1/z∈UM1/z\in U_{M}. Equivalently z∈ΩΔz\in\Omega_{\Delta}, where ΩΔ\Omega_{\Delta} is as in Theorem 6.

Now let GG satisfy Δ⁡(G)≤Δ\Delta(G)\leq\Delta. By Theorem 6, D⁡(G,z)≠0D(G,z)\neq 0 for all z∈ΩΔz\in\Omega_{\Delta}. In particular, D⁡(G,z)≠0D(G,z)\neq 0 for all zz with |z|≥r|z|\geq r and |arg⁡(z)|<θ|\argu(z)|<\theta. ∎

Theorems 5 through 7 highlight a general theme: domination polynomials inherit zero-free regions from hypergraph independence polynomials through the transformation (2.1). The results of [5] are optimal in several senses, so the explicit thresholds in Theorems 5 and 6 are unlikely to be significantly improved without incorporating additional structure of the specific closed neighborhood hypergraphs that arise from graphs. Identifying graph classes whose closed neighborhood hypergraphs have stronger analytic properties is an attractive direction.

4. Perspective 2: overlap-corrected inequalities for unimodality

This section develops lower bounds on rk​(G)r_{k}(G) by bounding the number of non-dominating kk-element subsets of V⁡(G)V(G). The novelty is an overlap correction that strengthens the naive union bound in graphs with repeated or highly overlapping neighborhoods. One of the two key statistics controlling this behavior is the following:

Definition 8.

For 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, define

(4.1) σk​(G):=∑v∈V⁡(G)(n−|N⁡[v]|k)(nk),\sigma_{k}(G):=\sum_{v\in V(G)}\frac{\binom{n-|N[v]|}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},

Now fix a graph GG on nn vertices and an integer 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n. For each v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G) define

Av:={S⊆V(G):|S|=k,S∩N[v]=∅}.A_{v}:=\{S\subseteq V(G):|S|=k,\ S\cap N[v]=\varnothing\}.

If S∈AvS\in A_{v}, then SS is not a dominating set because it does not contain vv or any of its neighbors. Consequently, the family of non-dominating kk-element sets is contained in ⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}. A direct union bound on ⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v} yields the following inequality.

Proposition 9.

For every graph GG on nn vertices and every kk,

dk​(G)≥(nk)−∑v∈V⁡(G)(n−|N⁡[v]|k).\displaystyle d_{k}(G)\geq\binom{n}{k}-\sum_{v\in V(G)}\binom{n-|N[v]|}{k}.

Equivalently, rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G).

Proof.

Every non-dominating kk-element set lies in ⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}, hence dk​(G)≥(nk)−|⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|.d_{k}(G)\geq\binom{n}{k}-\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|. For each vv, the sets in AvA_{v} are precisely the kk-element subsets of V⁡(G)∖N⁡[v]V(G)\setminus N[v], so |Av|=(n−|N⁡[v]|k)|A_{v}|=\binom{n-|N[v]|}{k}. Substituting together with |⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|≤∑v∈V⁡(G)|Av||\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}|\leq\sum_{v\in V(G)}|A_{v}| completes the proof. ∎

The quantity σk​(G)\sigma_{k}(G) depends on the entire multiset of neighborhood sizes. It can be bounded in terms of a simpler degree sequence proxy

(4.2) σ⁡(G):=∑v∈V⁡(G)2−deg⁡(v)−1\sigma(G):=\sum_{v\in V(G)}2^{-\deg(v)-1}

as established in the following proposition.

Proposition 10.

Let GG be a graph on nn vertices and set k=⌊n/2⌋k=\lfloor n/2\rfloor. Then σk​(G)≤2​σ​(G)\sigma_{k}(G)\leq 2\sigma(G).

Proof.

Fix mm with 1≤m≤n1\leq m\leq n. We claim

(4.3) (n−mk)(nk)≤21−m.\frac{\binom{n-m}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\leq 2^{1-m}.

Assume (n−mk)≠0\binom{n-m}{k}\neq 0 (otherwise the desired inequality is immediate). Using factorials and canceling yields

(n−mk)(nk)=(n−m)!​(n−k)!n!​(n−m−k)!=∏i=0m−1n−k−in−i.\frac{\binom{n-m}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}=\frac{(n-m)!(n-k)!}{n!(n-m-k)!}=\prod_{i=0}^{m-1}\frac{n-k-i}{\,n-i\,}.

If nn is even, then n=2​tn=2t and k=tk=t, so each factor equals (t−i)/(2​t−i)≤12(t-i)/(2t-i)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}, hence the product is at most 2−m≤21−m2^{-m}\leq 2^{1-m}. If nn is odd, then n=2​t+1n=2t+1 and k=tk=t, so the factors are (t+1−i)/(2​t+1−i)(t+1-i)/(2t+1-i); for i≥1i\geq 1 we have (t+1−i)/(2​t+1−i)≤12(t+1-i)/(2t+1-i)\leq\tfrac{1}{2}, while the remaining factor (t+1)/(2​t+1)≤1(t+1)/(2t+1)\leq 1, so for m≥2m\geq 2 the product is at most 1⋅2−(m−1)=21−m1\cdot 2^{-(m-1)}=2^{1-m}, and for m=1m=1 we have (t+1)/(2​t+1)≤1=20(t+1)/(2t+1)\leq 1=2^{0}. In all cases, (n−mk)/(nk)≤21−m\binom{n-m}{k}/\binom{n}{k}\leq 2^{1-m} as claimed. Now applying (4.3) with m=|N⁡[v]|=deg⁡(v)+1m=|N[v]|=\deg(v)+1 gives (n−|N⁡[v]|k)/(nk)≤2−deg⁡(v)\binom{n-|N[v]|}{k}/\binom{n}{k}\leq 2^{-\deg(v)}. Summing over vv yields σk​(G)≤∑v∈V⁡(G)2−deg⁡(v)=2​∑v∈V⁡(G)2−deg⁡(v)−1=2​σ​(G)\sigma_{k}(G)\leq\sum_{v\in V(G)}2^{-\deg(v)}=2\sum_{v\in V(G)}2^{-\deg(v)-1}=2\sigma(G). ∎

Combining Proposition 9 with the Beaton-Brown criterion yields unimodality whenever σk​(G)\sigma_{k}(G) is sufficiently small at k≈n/2k\approx n/2. The next proposition is a convenient degree sequence sufficient condition.

Proposition 11.

Let GG be a graph on n≥6n\geq 6 vertices and set k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil. If σ⁡(G)≤1/(n+2)\sigma(G)\leq 1/(n+2), then D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) is unimodal with mode kk.

Proof.

Let k0=⌊n/2⌋k_{0}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor. By Proposition 9 and Proposition 10,

1−rk0​(G)≤σk0​(G)≤2​σ​(G)≤2n+2.1-r_{k_{0}}(G)\leq\sigma_{k_{0}}(G)\leq 2\sigma(G)\leq\frac{2}{n+2}.

By monotonicity of rk​(G)r_{k}(G) (Proposition 2(i)), rk​(G)≥rk0​(G)≥1−2n+2=nn+2r_{k}(G)\geq r_{k_{0}}(G)\geq 1-\frac{2}{n+2}=\frac{n}{n+2}. A direct check shows that for n≥6n\geq 6 and k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil one has nn+2≥n−kk+1\frac{n}{n+2}\geq\frac{n-k}{k+1}. Therefore the Beaton-Brown tail criterion applies and yields unimodality with mode kk. ∎

One advantage of Proposition 11 is that it is sensitive to the entire degree sequence and is stable under adding universal vertices (that is, vertices vv for which N⁡[v]=V⁡(G)N[v]=V(G)).

Corollary 12.

Let GG be a graph on n≥6n\geq 6 vertices with mm universal vertices, and suppose every other vertex has degree at least δ\delta. If

(n−m)⋅2−δ−1≤1n+2,(n-m)\cdot 2^{-\delta-1}\leq\frac{1}{n+2},

then D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) is unimodal with mode ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil.

Proof.

Each universal vertex contributes 2−(n−1)−1=2−n2^{-(n-1)-1}=2^{-n} to σ⁡(G)\sigma(G), while each non-universal vertex contributes at most 2−δ−12^{-\delta-1}. Thus

σ⁡(G)≤m⋅2−n+(n−m)⋅2−δ−1≤(n−m)⋅2−δ−1+m2n.\sigma(G)\leq m\cdot 2^{-n}+(n-m)\cdot 2^{-\delta-1}\leq(n-m)\cdot 2^{-\delta-1}+\frac{m}{2^{n}}.

The hypothesis implies σ⁡(G)≤1/(n+2)\sigma(G)\leq 1/(n+2), so Proposition 11 yields the claim. ∎

As a baseline comparison, we refine the result of Beaton and Brown proving unimodality when δ⁡(G)≥2​log2​n\delta(G)\geq 2\log_{2}n [2].

Proposition 13.

Let GG be a graph on n≥4n\geq 4 vertices. If

δ⁡(G)≥log2⁡(n⁡(n+2))−2,\delta(G)\ \geq\ \log_{2}(n(n+2))-2,

then D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) is unimodal with mode ⌈n/2⌉\lceil n/2\rceil.

Proof.

Let k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil. By Proposition 9, 1−rk​(G)≤σk​(G)≤n⋅(n−δ⁡(G)−1k)(nk).1-r_{k}(G)\leq\sigma_{k}(G)\leq n\cdot\frac{\binom{n-\delta(G)-1}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}. Let m=δ⁡(G)+1m=\delta(G)+1. Using (n−mk)/(nk)=(n−km)/(nm)\binom{n-m}{k}/\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n-k}{m}/\binom{n}{m} and bounding as in the proof of Proposition 10 yields (n−mk)(nk)≤2−m.\frac{\binom{n-m}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}\leq 2^{-m}. Hence 1−rk​(G)≤n⋅2−δ⁡(G)−11-r_{k}(G)\leq n\cdot 2^{-\delta(G)-1}. Under the hypothesis δ⁡(G)≥log2⁡(n⁡(n+2))−2\delta(G)\geq\log_{2}(n(n+2))-2, this gives 1−rk​(G)≤2n+21-r_{k}(G)\leq\frac{2}{n+2} and so rk​(G)≥nn+2≥n−kk+1r_{k}(G)\geq\frac{n}{n+2}\geq\frac{n-k}{k+1}. The Beaton-Brown tail criterion yields unimodality with mode kk. ∎

The union bound in Proposition 9 ignores overlaps among the events AvA_{v}. We now introduce an overlap correction based on spanning trees, which is particularly effective when many vertices have similar closed neighborhoods. For 0≤k≤n0\leq k\leq n, define

(4.4) τk​(G):=max⁡∑u​v∈E⁡(T)T⁡(n−|N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|k)(nk),\tau_{k}(G):=\max_{T}\ \sum_{uv\in E(T)}\frac{\binom{n-|N[u]\cup N[v]|}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}},

where the maximum ranges over all spanning trees TT on the vertex set V⁡(G)V(G). The edges u​vuv of TT are not required to be edges of GG; the parameter is measuring overlap among the families AvA_{v}, and for this purpose only the vertex set matters. It is helpful to view τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) as a combinatorial optimization problem. Define weights on unordered pairs {u,v}\{u,v\} by wk​(u,v):=(n−|N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|k)(nk)=|Au∩Av|(nk).w_{k}(u,v):=\frac{\binom{n-|N[u]\cup N[v]|}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}=\frac{|A_{u}\cap A_{v}|}{\binom{n}{k}}. Then τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) is the maximum total weight of a spanning tree in the complete graph on V⁡(G)V(G) with these weights. In particular, τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) can be computed in polynomial time by a maximum spanning tree algorithm.

The extreme case that motivates the definition is when two vertices have identical closed neighborhoods. If N⁡[u]=N⁡[v]N[u]=N[v] then Au=AvA_{u}=A_{v} and therefore |Au∩Av|=|Au||A_{u}\cap A_{v}|=|A_{u}|. If a graph contains a large class of vertices with identical closed neighborhood, the union bound counts the same event many times, while the spanning tree subtraction in Proposition 14 can cancel all but one copy, making the bound essentially sharp on that twin class.

Proposition 14.

For every graph GG on nn vertices and every kk, rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)+τk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G)+\tau_{k}(G).

Proof.

We use the notation AvA_{v} from Proposition 9. Fix any spanning tree TT on V⁡(G)V(G) and choose a leaf ℓ\ell of TT with unique neighbor ww in TT. Let U=⋃v∈V⁡(G)∖{ℓ}AvU=\bigcup_{v\in V(G)\setminus\{\ell\}}A_{v}. Then |⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|=|U|+|Aℓ|−|U∩Aℓ|.\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|=|U|+|A_{\ell}|-|U\cap A_{\ell}|. Since Aw⊆UA_{w}\subseteq U, we have U∩Aℓ⊇Aw∩AℓU\cap A_{\ell}\supseteq A_{w}\cap A_{\ell}, and therefore |⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|≤|U|+|Aℓ|−|Aw∩Aℓ|.\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|\leq|U|+|A_{\ell}|-|A_{w}\cap A_{\ell}|. Applying the same argument to UU along the spanning tree obtained from TT by deleting ℓ\ell, and iterating until all vertices are deleted, yields |⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|≤∑v∈V⁡(G)|Av|−∑u​v∈E⁡(T)|Au∩Av|.\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|\leq\sum_{v\in V(G)}|A_{v}|-\sum_{uv\in E(T)}|A_{u}\cap A_{v}|. This inequality holds for every spanning tree TT, hence

(4.5) |⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|≤∑v∈V⁡(G)|Av|−max⁡∑u​v∈E⁡(T)T⁡|Au∩Av|.\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|\leq\sum_{v\in V(G)}|A_{v}|-\max_{T}\sum_{uv\in E(T)}|A_{u}\cap A_{v}|.

Now, as in Proposition 9, dk​(G)≥(nk)−|⋃v∈V⁡(G)Av|.d_{k}(G)\geq\binom{n}{k}-\left|\bigcup_{v\in V(G)}A_{v}\right|. For each vv we have |Av|=(n−|N⁡[v]|k)|A_{v}|=\binom{n-|N[v]|}{k}, and for each pair u,vu,v we have |Au∩Av|=(n−|N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|k)|A_{u}\cap A_{v}|=\binom{n-|N[u]\cup N[v]|}{k}. Substituting into the inequality in (4.5) and dividing by (nk)\binom{n}{k} gives rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)+τk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G)+\tau_{k}(G). ∎

Combining Proposition 14 with the Beaton-Brown tail criterion gives an overlap-corrected sufficient condition for unimodality at k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil.

Theorem 15.

Let GG be a graph on nn vertices and let k=⌈n/2⌉k=\lceil n/2\rceil. If

(4.6) σk​(G)−τk​(G)≤2​k+1−nk+1,\sigma_{k}(G)-\tau_{k}(G)\ \leq\ \frac{2k+1-n}{k+1},

then D⁡(G,x)D(G,x) is unimodal with mode kk.

Proof.

By Proposition 14, rk​(G)≥1−σk​(G)+τk​(G)r_{k}(G)\geq 1-\sigma_{k}(G)+\tau_{k}(G). Rearranging (4.6) gives 1−σk​(G)+τk​(G)≥n−kk+1,1-\sigma_{k}(G)+\tau_{k}(G)\ \geq\ \frac{n-k}{k+1}, so rk​(G)≥(n−k)/(k+1)r_{k}(G)\geq(n-k)/(k+1). The Beaton-Brown tail criterion implies dk​(G)≥dk+1​(G)≥⋯≥dn​(G)d_{k}(G)\geq d_{k+1}(G)\geq\cdots\geq d_{n}(G), and together with the monotonicity of rk​(G)r_{k}(G) this yields unimodality with mode kk. ∎

We now give a concrete family of graphs were our phenomena apply. The key property is that any graph in the family contains a large twin class inside a clique, so the spanning tree subtraction encoded by τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) cancels essentially the entire union bound contribution of that class (as discussed following (4.4)), leaving a single binomial ratio that can be controlled using (4.3).

In that light, fix integers s≥2s\geq 2 and N≥1N\geq 1. Let CC and QQ be disjoint cliques on NN and ss vertices, respectively. Choose distinguished vertices c0∈Cc_{0}\in C and q0∈Qq_{0}\in Q, and form a graph G=GN,sG=G_{N,s} by adding the edges c0​qc_{0}q for all q∈Q∖{q0}q\in Q\setminus\{q_{0}\} and write n:=|V⁡(GN,s)|=N+sn:=|V(G_{N,s})|=N+s (see Figure 1 for an illustration).

Begin by evaluating σk​(G)\sigma_{k}(G) from definition (4.1). For any c∈C∖{c0}c\in C\setminus\{c_{0}\} we have N⁡[c]=CN[c]=C, hence n−|N⁡[c]|=s<kn-|N[c]|=s<k and so (n−|N⁡[c]|k)=0\binom{n-|N[c]|}{k}=0 by our binomial convention. The vertex c0c_{0} satisfies N⁡[c0]=V⁡(G)∖{q0}N[c_{0}]=V(G)\setminus\{q_{0}\}, giving n−|N⁡[c0]|=1<kn-|N[c_{0}]|=1<k and therefore contributing 00 as well. On the QQ side, the vertex q0q_{0} has N⁡[q0]=QN[q_{0}]=Q, so n−|N⁡[q0]|=Nn-|N[q_{0}]|=N, while every q∈Q∖{q0}q\in Q\setminus\{q_{0}\} has N⁡[q]=Q∪{c0}N[q]=Q\cup\{c_{0}\}, so n−|N⁡[q]|=N−1n-|N[q]|=N-1. Summing the resulting terms in (4.1) yields σk​(G)=((Nk)+(s−1)​(N−1k))/(nk)\sigma_{k}(G)=\left(\binom{N}{k}+(s-1)\binom{N-1}{k}\right)/\binom{n}{k}.

Now for τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G), use the weight interpretation following (4.4). If u∈C∖{c0}u\in C\setminus\{c_{0}\} then N⁡[u]=CN[u]=C, so N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]N[u]\cup N[v] contains CC for every v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), and therefore the complement V⁡(G)∖(N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v])V(G)\setminus(N[u]\cup N[v]) is contained in QQ and has size at most s<ks<k, forcing wk​(u,v)=(n−|N⁡[u]∪N⁡[v]|k)/(nk)=0w_{k}(u,v)=\binom{n-|N[u]\cup N[v]|}{k}/\binom{n}{k}=0 for every vv. Likewise if u=c0u=c_{0} then N⁡[c0]=V⁡(G)∖{q0}N[c_{0}]=V(G)\setminus\{q_{0}\} implies n−|N⁡[c0]∪N⁡[v]|≤1<kn-|N[c_{0}]\cup N[v]|\leq 1<k and again wk​(c0,v)=0w_{k}(c_{0},v)=0 for all vv. Hence the only potentially nonzero weights occur between pairs of vertices in QQ. For any distinct q,q′∈Q∖{q0}q,q^{\prime}\in Q\setminus\{q_{0}\} we have N⁡[q]=N⁡[q′]=Q∪{c0}N[q]=N[q^{\prime}]=Q\cup\{c_{0}\}, so n−|N⁡[q]∪N⁡[q′]|=N−1n-|N[q]\cup N[q^{\prime}]|=N-1; also N⁡[q0]⊆N⁡[q]N[q_{0}]\subseteq N[q] for q∈Q∖{q0}q\in Q\setminus\{q_{0}\}, so n−|N⁡[q0]∪N⁡[q]|=N−1n-|N[q_{0}]\cup N[q]|=N-1 as well. Thus every edge in the complete graph on vertex set QQ has weight (N−1k)/(nk)\binom{N-1}{k}/\binom{n}{k}, while every edge incident to a vertex in CC in the complete graph on V⁡(G)V(G) has weight 00. A spanning tree on V⁡(G)V(G) can contain at most s−1s-1 edges with both ends in QQ, and taking any spanning tree on QQ together with NN additional edges connecting the vertices of CC to QQ achieves s−1s-1 such edges, so the maximum total weight is (s−1)​(N−1k)/(nk)(s-1)\binom{N-1}{k}/\binom{n}{k}, and hence this is τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G). It follows that σk​(G)−τk​(G)=(Nk)(nk).\sigma_{k}(G)-\tau_{k}(G)=\frac{\binom{N}{k}}{\binom{n}{k}}.

Now for each integer ℓ≥4\ell\geq 4, we claim the graph GN,ℓG_{N,\ell} with N=2ℓ−ℓ−2N=2^{\ell}-\ell-2 has unimodal domination polynomial with mode k=n/2k=n/2 where n=2ℓ−2n=2^{\ell}-2. On the other hand, since n=2​kn=2k the right-hand side of (4.6) is (2​k+1−n)/(k+1)=1/(k+1)(2k+1-n)/(k+1)=1/(k+1), and with n=2ℓ−2n=2^{\ell}-2 we have k+1=2ℓ−1k+1=2^{\ell-1}, hence 1/(k+1)=21−ℓ1/(k+1)=2^{1-\ell}. Therefore (4.6) holds, and Theorem 15 then implies D⁡(GN,ℓ,x)D(G_{N,\ell},x) is unimodal with mode kk.

5. Perspective 3: Total Positivity

Our last perspective shows that inheriting theory from enumerative combinatorics is a fruitful endeavor for uncovering the unimodality of domination polynomials. We start by showing a broad class of polynomials have log-concave, and hence unimodal, domination sequences. This is done by appealing to the theory of total positivity, particularly appealing to a classical result of Lindström-Gessel-Viennot on positivity and lattice paths in the plane. We then see how a ubiquitous class of graphs, threshold graphs, have domination polynomials in this broad class of polynomials, and therefore have unimodal domination polynomials.

Lemma 16.

Let α1≥α2≥⋯≥αm≥1\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\alpha_{m}\geq 1 and 0≤β1<β2<⋯<βm0\leq\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}<\cdots<\beta_{m} be integers such that

αr+1+βr+1=αr+βr+1for all ​r=1,…,m−1.\alpha_{r+1}+\beta_{r+1}=\alpha_{r}+\beta_{r}+1\qquad\text{for all }r=1,\dots,m-1.

Define P⁡(x):=∑r=1mxαr​(1+x)βr.P(x):=\sum_{r=1}^{m}x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}}. Then the coefficient sequence of P⁡(x)P(x) is unimodal.

Proof.

Set nr:=αr+βrn_{r}:=\alpha_{r}+\beta_{r} for 1≤r≤m1\leq r\leq m. The hypothesis implies nr+1=nr+1n_{r+1}=n_{r}+1, and hence nr=n1+(r−1)n_{r}=n_{1}+(r-1), for all rr. In particular N:=nm=n1+(m−1).N:=n_{m}=n_{1}+(m-1). Since deg⁡(xαr​(1+x)βr)=nr\deg\bigl(x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}}\bigr)=n_{r}, it follows that deg⁡P=N\deg P=N because the top degree term xαm+βmx^{\alpha_{m}+\beta_{m}} from xαm​(1+x)βmx^{\alpha_{m}}(1+x)^{\beta_{m}} has no cancellation. Writing P⁡(x)=∑k=0Nck​xk,P(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{N}c_{k}x^{k}, we expand each summand:

xαr​(1+x)βr=xαr​∑j=0βr(βrj)​xj=∑j=0βr(βrj)​xαr+j.x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}}=x^{\alpha_{r}}\sum_{j=0}^{\beta_{r}}\binom{\beta_{r}}{j}x^{j}=\sum_{j=0}^{\beta_{r}}\binom{\beta_{r}}{j}x^{\alpha_{r}+j}.

With the convention (nt)=0\binom{n}{t}=0 when t∉{0,1,…,n}t\notin\{0,1,\dots,n\}, we have for every 0≤k≤N0\leq k\leq N,

(5.1) ck:=[xk]​P​(x)=∑r=1m(βrk−αr).c_{k}:=[x^{k}]P(x)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom{\beta_{r}}{\,k-\alpha_{r}\,}.

The sequence (c0,c1,…,cN)(c_{0},c_{1},\dots,c_{N}) has no internal zeros. Indeed, each term xαr​(1+x)βrx^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}} has lowest degree term xαrx^{\alpha_{r}} which has degree at least αm\alpha_{m}, so ck=0c_{k}=0 for k<αmk<\alpha_{m}. On the other hand, the final summand xαm​(1+x)βmx^{\alpha_{m}}(1+x)^{\beta_{m}} has support on all degrees αm,αm+1,…,αm+βm\alpha_{m},\alpha_{m}+1,\dots,\alpha_{m}+\beta_{m}, and since αm+βm=nm=N\alpha_{m}+\beta_{m}=n_{m}=N, we obtain ck>0c_{k}>0 for all αm≤k≤N\alpha_{m}\leq k\leq N.

To prove unimodality, we show log-concavity:

(5.2) ck2≥ck−1​ck+1(0≤k≤N),c_{k}^{2}\geq c_{k-1}c_{k+1}\qquad(0\leq k\leq N),

interpreting c−1=cN+1=0c_{-1}=c_{N+1}=0. Log-concavity together with the absence of internal zeros implies unimodality (see [17]). We obtain (5.2) by encoding the coefficients as path counts in a planar acyclic network and applying the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma [10, 14] together with a planar noncrossing argument from total positivity (see [16]).

Consider the directed grid graph on ℤ2\mathbb{Z}^{2} with edges (i,j)→(i+1,j)(i,j)\to(i+1,j) and (i,j)→(i,j+1)(i,j)\to(i,j+1) (steps east or north). For 0≤k≤N0\leq k\leq N, define sinks on the diagonal x+y=N+1x+y=N+1 by

Bk:=(k,N−k+1).B_{k}:=(k,\,N-k+1).

For 1≤r≤m1\leq r\leq m, define vertices

Ur:=(αr,m−r+1),Vr:=(αr+1,m−r),U_{r}:=(\alpha_{r},\,m-r+1),\qquad V_{r}:=(\alpha_{r}+1,\,m-r),

and adjoin two additional sources ss and tt, with directed edges s→Urs\to U_{r} and t→Vrt\to V_{r} for each rr. We embed this as a planar network in the evident way: the grid is planar, we place ss above tt to the left, and we draw the edges s→Urs\to U_{r} and t→Vrt\to V_{r} as noncrossing arcs. Let p⁡(X,Y)p(X,Y) denote the number of directed paths from XX to YY in this network.

We compute the number of paths from UrU_{r} and VrV_{r} to BkB_{k}. A directed path from Ur=(αr,m−r+1)U_{r}=(\alpha_{r},m-r+1) to Bk=(k,N−k+1)B_{k}=(k,N-k+1) must take E=k−αrE=k-\alpha_{r} east steps and

N′=(N−k+1)−(m−r+1)=N−k−m+rN^{\prime}=(N-k+1)-(m-r+1)=N-k-m+r

north steps. Since N=nr+(m−r)N=n_{r}+(m-r), we have N′=nr−kN^{\prime}=n_{r}-k. The total number of steps is then

E+N′=(k−αr)+(nr−k)=nr−αr=βr,E+N^{\prime}=(k-\alpha_{r})+(n_{r}-k)=n_{r}-\alpha_{r}=\beta_{r},

and the number of such paths is (E+N′E)=(βrk−αr)\binom{E+N^{\prime}}{E}=\binom{\beta_{r}}{k-\alpha_{r}}. Thus p⁡(Ur,Bk)=(βrk−αr)p(U_{r},B_{k})=\binom{\beta_{r}}{k-\alpha_{r}}. Similarly, a directed path from Vr=(αr+1,m−r)V_{r}=(\alpha_{r}+1,m-r) to BkB_{k} must take E=k−αr−1E=k-\alpha_{r}-1 east steps and

N′=(N−k+1)−(m−r)=N−k−m+r+1=nr−k+1N^{\prime}=(N-k+1)-(m-r)=N-k-m+r+1=n_{r}-k+1

north steps, so again the total number of steps is βr\beta_{r} and p⁡(Vr,Bk)=(βrk−αr−1)p(V_{r},B_{k})=\binom{\beta_{r}}{k-\alpha_{r}-1}. Every path from ss to BkB_{k} first chooses one edge s→Urs\to U_{r} for some rr then follows a path from that UrU_{r} to BkB_{k}, so

p⁡(s,Bk)=∑r=1mp⁡(Ur,Bk)=∑r=1m(βrk−αr)=ckp(s,B_{k})=\sum_{r=1}^{m}p(U_{r},B_{k})=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom{\beta_{r}}{k-\alpha_{r}}=c_{k}

by (5.1). Likewise,

p⁡(t,Bk)=∑r=1mp⁡(Vr,Bk)=∑r=1m(βrk−αr−1)=ck−1,p(t,B_{k})=\sum_{r=1}^{m}p(V_{r},B_{k})=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\binom{\beta_{r}}{k-\alpha_{r}-1}=c_{k-1},

and similarly p⁡(s,Bk+1)=ck+1p(s,B_{k+1})=c_{k+1} and p⁡(t,Bk+1)=ckp(t,B_{k+1})=c_{k}.

Now fix kk with 0≤k≤N−10\leq k\leq N-1 and consider the 2×22\times 2 determinant

Δk:=det(p⁡(s,Bk)p⁡(s,Bk+1)p⁡(t,Bk)p⁡(t,Bk+1))=det(ckck+1ck−1ck)=ck2−ck−1​ck+1.\Delta_{k}:=\det\begin{pmatrix}p(s,B_{k})&p(s,B_{k+1})\\ p(t,B_{k})&p(t,B_{k+1})\end{pmatrix}=\det\begin{pmatrix}c_{k}&c_{k+1}\\ c_{k-1}&c_{k}\end{pmatrix}=c_{k}^{2}-c_{k-1}c_{k+1}.

By the Lindström–Gessel–Viennot lemma for two sources and two sinks [10, 14], Δk\Delta_{k} equals the number of vertex-disjoint path pairs (s→Bk,t→Bk+1)(s\to B_{k},\ t\to B_{k+1}) minus the number of vertex-disjoint path pairs (s→Bk+1,t→Bk)(s\to B_{k+1},\ t\to B_{k}). In our planar embedding, ss lies above tt on the left, while BkB_{k} lies above Bk+1B_{k+1} on the right. A planar noncrossing argument shows that there are no vertex-disjoint path pairs connecting ss to the lower sink Bk+1B_{k+1} and tt to the upper sink BkB_{k}: such a pair would force a crossing in the plane, which is impossible for vertex-disjoint directed paths in this acyclic planar network. Consequently the second term vanishes and Δk≥0\Delta_{k}\geq 0. Therefore ck2≥ck−1​ck+1c_{k}^{2}\geq c_{k-1}c_{k+1} for 0≤k≤N−10\leq k\leq N-1, and with the boundary convention c−1=cN+1=0c_{-1}=c_{N+1}=0 the same holds for k=0k=0 and k=Nk=N. Thus (c0,c1,…,cN)(c_{0},c_{1},\ldots,c_{N}) is log-concave. The result follows since the sequence has no internal zeros. ∎

Lemma 16 paves the way for proving that the domination polynomials of threshold graphs are unimodal. We first recall how this ubiquitous class of graphs is constructed. A graph TT on nn vertices is a threshold graph if there is an ordering of the vertex set v1,…,vnv_{1},\dots,v_{n} such that for each jj the vertex vjv_{j} is either isolated or dominating in the induced subgraph on {v1,…,vj−1,vj}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{j-1},v_{j}\}. We call such an ordering a threshold ordering. In a threshold ordering, the vertices added as dominating themselves form a clique and the vertices added as isolated form an independent set. We refer to these vertices throughout as vertices on the dominating side and vertices on the independent side, respectively. The structure of neighborhoods is closely connected to these sets. For instance, neighborhoods from the independent side into the clique side are nested: if uu and ww are vertices on the independent side with uu earlier than ww in the ordering, and CC is the set of vertices on the dominating side, then N⁡(u)∩C⊇N⁡(w)∩CN(u)\cap C\supseteq N(w)\cap C. See [15] for these standard properties.

Fix a threshold ordering v1,…,vnv_{1},\dots,v_{n}. List the vertices on the dominating side, in the order they appear, as c1,…,cmc_{1},\dots,c_{m}. Write trt_{r} for the index with cr=vtrc_{r}=v_{t_{r}}. For each rr write Pr={v1,…,vtr−1}P_{r}=\{v_{1},\dots,v_{t_{r}-1}\}, the vertices in TT appearing before crc_{r} does. Let II be the set of vertices that were added on the isolated side. For each rr, let Ir⊆II_{r}\subseteq I be the set of vertices on the isolated side that appear after crc_{r} in the threshold ordering, so Ir={vj∈I:j>tr}I_{r}=\{v_{j}\in I:j>t_{r}\}. The next lemma shows that dominating sets can be partitioned by their last vertex on the dominating side in the threshold ordering.

Lemma 17.

Let TT be a threshold graph with a fixed threshold ordering as above. Every dominating set SS that contains at least one vertex from the dominating side of the threshold ordering of TT has a unique index rr such that crc_{r} is the last vertex on the dominating side of the threshold ordering that lies in SS, and for this rr one has

S=U∪{cr}∪IrS=U\cup\{c_{r}\}\cup I_{r}

for an arbitrary subset U⊆PrU\subseteq P_{r}. A dominating set of TT that contains no vertex from the dominating side of the threshold ordering exists if and only if there is at least one vertex on the isolated side of TT before c1c_{1}, and in that case the only such dominating set is the set of all vertices on the isolated side.

To illustrate Lemma 17, consider the threshold graph TT with vertices v1,v2,…,v14v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{14} listed in threshold order, whose dominating side consists of the vertices {v3,v5,v9,v11}\{v_{3},v_{5},v_{9},v_{11}\}, so c1=v3,c2=v5,c3=v9,c_{1}=v_{3},\ c_{2}=v_{5},\ c_{3}=v_{9}, and v11=c4v_{11}=c_{4}. The graph TT is illustrated in Figure 2.

An example of a dominating set is S={v3,v4,v5,v8,v9,v10,v12,v13,v14}S=\{v_{3},v_{4},v_{5},v_{8},v_{9},v_{10},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14}\}. Notice that c3=v9c_{3}=v_{9} is the last vertex in SS on the dominating side (in threshold order). So we if decompose SS as {v3,v4,v5,v8}∪{v9}∪{v10,v12,v13,v14}\{v_{3},v_{4},v_{5},v_{8}\}\cup\{v_{9}\}\cup\{v_{10},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14}\} we have SS is of the form U∪{c3}∪I3U\cup\{c_{3}\}\cup I_{3} because I3={v10,v12,v13,v14}I_{3}=\{v_{10},v_{12},v_{13},v_{14}\}. The vertices in I3I_{3} have to be in SS because c3=v9c_{3}=v_{9} is the last vertex on the dominating side that is in SS, so all vertices after it in threshold order that are on the independent side must be in it. Moreover U⊆{v1,v2,…,v8}=P3U\subseteq\{v_{1},v_{2},\ldots,v_{8}\}=P_{3}. Replacing UU with any subset of P3P_{3} will keep SS dominating because c3=v9c_{3}=v_{9} is adjacent to all vertices in P3P_{3}.

Proof of Lemma 17.

Let SS be a dominating set containing at least one vertex on the dominating side and let crc_{r} be the last vertex on the dominating side in the threshold ordering that is also in SS. Consider a vertex ww on the isolated side that appears after crc_{r} in threshold order. At the moment ww is added in the threshold construction it is isolated from the previously built graph, so ww has no neighbors among {v1,…,vtr}\{v_{1},\dots,v_{t_{r}}\}. Since all other vertices on the dominating side appear after cr=vtrc_{r}=v_{t_{r}}, and crc_{r} is the last vertex on the dominating side in SS, the set SS contains no vertex on the dominating side that dominates ww. Thus ww must belong to SS. This shows Ir⊆SI_{r}\subseteq S and also cr∈Sc_{r}\in S.

Every vertex in the prefix PrP_{r} is adjacent to crc_{r} because crc_{r} was added as a vertex on the dominating side, so crc_{r} dominates all vertices of PrP_{r}. Every vertex csc_{s} on the dominating side with s>rs>r is adjacent to crc_{r} because each vertex on the dominating side is adjacent to all earlier vertices. Thus every vertex outside IrI_{r} is dominated by crc_{r}. It follows that any set of the form {cr}∪Ir∪U\{c_{r}\}\cup I_{r}\cup U with U⊆PrU\subseteq P_{r} is dominating. Conversely, we have already shown that a dominating set SS with last vertex crc_{r} on the dominating side must contain {cr}∪Ir\{c_{r}\}\cup I_{r}, and any additional vertices of SS must come from PrP_{r}. Therefore S={cr}∪Ir∪US=\{c_{r}\}\cup I_{r}\cup U for some U⊆PrU\subseteq P_{r}. The index rr is unique because the last vertex on the dominating side in a given set is unique.

If SS contains no vertex on the dominating side, then S⊆IS\subseteq I. Any vertex in I∖SI\setminus S has no neighbor in II, so this forces SS to be II. The set II dominates the first vertex c1c_{1} on the dominating side if and only if c1c_{1} has at least one neighbor in II, and in a threshold ordering c1c_{1} is adjacent precisely to the vertices that appear before it. Hence II is dominating if and only if there exists a vertex on the isolated side before c1c_{1}. ∎

Lemma 17 yields a closed form for the domination polynomial of a threshold graph.

Lemma 18.

Let TT be a threshold graph. Let c1,…,cmc_{1},\ldots,c_{m}, II, I1,…,ImI_{1},\ldots,I_{m} and P1,…,PmP_{1},\ldots,P_{m} be as in Lemma 17. Then

(5.3) D⁡(T,x)=∑r=1mxαr​(1+x)βr+ε​x|I|.D(T,x)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}}+\varepsilon x^{|I|}.

where for each 1≤r≤m1\leq r\leq m, βr=|Pr|\beta_{r}=|P_{r}|, αr=|Ir|+1\alpha_{r}=|I_{r}|+1, and ε∈{0,1}\varepsilon\in\{0,1\} is 11 if II is a dominating set and 00 otherwise.

Proof.

By Lemma 17,

D⁡(T,x)\displaystyle D(T,x) =∑S​ a dominating set x|S|=∑r=1m∑U⊆Prx|{cr}∪Ir∪U|+ε​x|I|\displaystyle=\sum_{S\text{ a dominating set }}x^{|S|}=\sum_{r=1}^{m}\sum_{U\subseteq P_{r}}x^{|\{c_{r}\}\cup I_{r}\cup U|}+\varepsilon x^{|I|}
=∑r=1mx|{cr∪Ir}|​(∑U⊆Prx|U|)+ε​x|I|=∑r=1mxαr​(1+x)βr+ε​x|I|.\displaystyle=\sum_{r=1}^{m}x^{|\{c_{r}\cup I_{r}\}|}\left(\sum_{U\subseteq P_{r}}x^{|U|}\right)+\varepsilon x^{|I|}=\sum_{r=1}^{m}x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}}+\varepsilon x^{|I|}.

∎

The parameters in (5.3) satisfy a rigid staircase condition. Write nr=αr+βrn_{r}=\alpha_{r}+\beta_{r} for the degree of the rrth binomial summand. Moving from crc_{r} to cr+1c_{r+1} shifts some vertices on the isolated side from the forced set IrI_{r} into the optional prefix Pr+1P_{r+1} and adds one additional optional vertex corresponding to crc_{r} itself entering the prefix. Concretely, if there are s≥0s\geq 0 on the isolated side between crc_{r} and cr+1c_{r+1} in the threshold ordering, then βr+1=βr+s+1\beta_{r+1}=\beta_{r}+s+1 and αr+1=αr−s\alpha_{r+1}=\alpha_{r}-s. Adding yields

(5.4) nr+1=nr+1.n_{r+1}=n_{r}+1.

We can now conclude unimodality for threshold graphs.

Theorem 19.

If TT is a threshold graph, then its domination polynomial D⁡(T,x)D(T,x) is unimodal.

Proof.

Fix a threshold ordering and write D⁡(T,x)D(T,x) in the form (5.3) from Lemma 18, using the same notation therein for the involved sets. If there are no vertices on the dominating side then D⁡(T,x)=ε​x|I|D(T,x)=\varepsilon x^{|I|}, which is a single monomial and hence unimodal, so assume m≥1m\geq 1. By construction one has α1≥α2≥⋯≥αm≥1\alpha_{1}\geq\alpha_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\alpha_{m}\geq 1 and 0≤β1<β2<⋯<βm0\leq\beta_{1}<\beta_{2}<\cdots<\beta_{m}, and the degrees nr:=αr+βrn_{r}:=\alpha_{r}+\beta_{r} satisfy the staircase condition (5.4). If ε=0\varepsilon=0, then D⁡(T,x)=∑r=1mxαr​(1+x)βrD(T,x)=\sum_{r=1}^{m}x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}} is exactly of the form required by Lemma 16, and therefore has a unimodal coefficient sequence. In this case Lemma 17 implies there is at least one vertex on the isolated side before c1c_{1}, hence P1⊆IP_{1}\subseteq I is nonempty and β1=|P1|≥1\beta_{1}=|P_{1}|\geq 1, so 0=β0<β10=\beta_{0}<\beta_{1}. Consequently, D⁡(T,x)=∑r=0mxαr​(1+x)βrD(T,x)=\sum_{r=0}^{m}x^{\alpha_{r}}(1+x)^{\beta_{r}} satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 16, and therefore the coefficient sequence of D⁡(T,x)D(T,x) is unimodal. ∎

6. Conclusion and further directions

The overaching theme in this article is that tools from outside of domination polynomial literature can pave the way for new and rich perspectives that expand our understanding of these polynomials, particularly in the lens of resolving their unimodality. The three perspectives developed in this paper point toward several avenues for extending these results while keeping in line with this overarching theme.

Perspective 1: Beyond closed neighborhoods. The identity (2.1) is a manifestation of a general principle: domination is a transversal condition in an associated hypergraph. Many variations in domination theory admit analogous hypergraph models, for example total domination (hitting open neighborhoods), distance-rr domination (hitting rr-neighborhoods), and domination in directed graphs. Each gives rise to a natural polynomial that enumerates dominating objects. It would be interesting to systematically develop reciprocity identities and to identify which zero-free regions for hypergraph independence polynomials can be transferred to these variants. In particular, one can ask for analogues of Theorems 5 and 6 for total domination polynomials and for distance domination polynomials in classes of bounded degree.

Perspective 2: Higher order overlap corrections. The spanning tree correction in Proposition 14 is a controlled inclusion–exclusion refinement that subtracts a collection of pairwise overlaps. In graphs with significant neighborhood repetition, such as graphs with large twin classes or nested neighborhoods, one expects higher-order overlaps to also be large. This suggests developing corrections based on larger structures (for example, bounded depth trees, hypertrees, or sparse complexes) that capture triple and higher intersections among the events AvA_{v}. Understanding the best possible overlap corrections for a given graph family, and how they interact with the Beaton-Brown criterion, is a promising direction for producing unimodality results in classes where the minimum degree is small but the neighborhood structure is highly redundant.

Perspective 3: Total positivity beyond threshold graphs. The threshold graph proof proceeds by decomposing dominating sets into disjoint families whose generating functions are shifted binomial rows forming a staircase. This invites the search for other graph classes admitting similar decompositions. A natural candidate for instance is split graphs, which are generalizations of threshold graphs. In such graphs it is plausible that dominating sets can be partitioned by the location of a “last” vertex in an appropriate ordering, producing sums of binomial pieces with controlled overlap. The algebraic Lemma 16 is robust and should apply whenever such a staircase structure can be established. Furthermore, it is possible that generalizations of Lindström-Gessel-Viennot such as that in the work of Hopkins and Zaimi (see [11]) can resolve unimodality for more general classes beyond threshold graphs.

Toward hereditary unimodality results. Conjecture 1 is open even for trees. The three perspectives suggest three different approaches to hereditary classes: through the analytic properties of the closed neighborhood hypergraph, through probabilistic estimates on neighborhood-avoidance events at k≈n/2k\approx n/2, and through explicit decompositions into unimodal polynomial pieces. It would be interesting to understand whether these approaches can be combined. For example, chordal graphs and interval graphs often admit elimination orderings that enforce nested neighborhood structure, and they also have closed neighborhood hypergraphs with constrained intersection patterns. Whether these features can be leveraged to build staircase decompositions or effective overlap corrections, and thereby prove unimodality for new hereditary classes, remains an appealing open problem.

Concrete questions. We close with a few concrete questions motivated by the methods above.

(1) For a fixed Δ\Delta, what is the best possible region in the complex plane that is guaranteed to be zero-free for all domination polynomials of graphs with maximum degree at most Δ\Delta? The transfer from [5] is optimal for general bounded degree hypergraphs, but the closed neighborhood hypergraphs ℋG\mathcal{H}_{G} satisfy strong additional constraints. Can those constraints be exploited to enlarge the zero-free region beyond what is possible for arbitrary hypergraphs of the same maximum degree?

(2) The quantity τk​(G)\tau_{k}(G) is defined through a maximum spanning tree problem and is therefore efficiently computable. Can one identify additional, efficiently computable corrections that incorporate higher-order overlaps and yield substantially stronger unimodality criteria on sparse graph classes such as trees?

(3) How much can total positivity afford us? For instance, is there a way to prove split graphs have unimodal domination polynomials using total positivity? Split graphs generalize threshold graphs by relaxing the nested neighborhood condition, so an affirmative answer would extend Theorem 19 to a significantly larger hereditary class. If not, can one use generalizations of Lindström-Gessel-Viennot such as in [11] to apply total positivity beyond threshold graphs?
